{"activityBriefs":[{"objectiveIds":["Recognize repeated-measures designs"],"title":"Design classifier","type":"retrieval_check","learnerAction":"Classify each study vignette as repeated-measures or between-subjects.","instructions":"Read the four vignettes and choose the design for each:
1) 4 participants solve the same puzzle in attempt 1, 2, and 3.
2) 36 participants are split into 3 groups; each group watches only one ad spot once and gives one rating.
3) 5 judges each rate the same 3 job applications on attractiveness.
4) 20 students take pretest and posttest on anxiety with the same scale.
For each, write one justification sentence.","successCriteria":"All four vignettes classified correctly: 1, 3, and 4 as repeated-measures; 2 as between-subjects, with justifications mentioning repeated observations per same case for RM designs.","feedbackGuidance":"If a learner misclassifies a design, clarify that repeated-measures requires linked observations for the same unit across conditions (same participant, same judge, same person measured multiple times). Between-subject designs require different participants per condition and independent observations. Emphasize that the core diagnostic is dependency versus independence of scores.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Compute RM means from wide data"],"title":"Match each mean symbol","type":"ordering_matching","learnerAction":"Match each symbol to the correct mean from the wide dataset.","instructions":"Using the tower-von-Hanoi data (Vp1–Vp4, Versuche 1–3), compute and match: Γ (grand mean), A1,A2,A3 (condition means), and P1..P4 (person means).
Data: 
Vp1: 10,5,3
Vp2: 6,4,2
Vp3: 11,9,4
Vp4: 7,4,1","successCriteria":"Correct mapping: Γ=5.5, A1=8.5, A2=5.5, A3=2.5, P1=6, P2=4, P3=8, P4=4.","feedbackGuidance":"If values are off, re-check definitions: A means are column means across participants; P means are row means across conditions; grand mean is the mean of all cells (or mean of all condition means/row means). Typical error is mixing up person means with condition means or forgetting there are 12 total values.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Decompose total variation in RM ANOVA"],"title":"Compute QS components","type":"practice_task","learnerAction":"Compute QS_A and QS_{A×Vpn} and label what each term represents.","instructions":"For example 1 with N=4 and p=3, use:
QS_A = N * Σ(A_i - G)^2
QS_{A×Vpn} = ΣΣ[x_im - (A_i + P_m - G)]^2.
Use the same means from the previous task.","successCriteria":"Both sums are correct: QS_A = 72, QS_{A×Vpn} = 6. Also correctly describe QS_A as systematic effect of condition/time and QS_{A×Vpn} as residual within-person variation (not-person variance).","feedbackGuidance":"If only one SS is provided, explain that RM ANOVA separates treatment-related systematic variation and person-adjusted residual variation. If the learner subtracts wrong expected value, remind the residual formula is x_im - (Ai + Pm - G), not x_im - Ai or x_im - G alone.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Compute df and mean squares"],"title":"Line up df and MQS values","type":"ordering_matching","learnerAction":"Match each formula to the correct numeric result for example 1.","instructions":"Match the quantity to its value: 
- df_A = p - 1
- df_{A×Vpn} = (N - 1)(p - 1)
- MQS_A = QS_A / df_A
- MQS_{A×Vpn} = QS_{A×Vpn} / df_{A×Vpn}
Given N=4, p=3, QS_A=72, QS_{A×Vpn}=6.","successCriteria":"Correct matches are: df_A=2, df_{A×Vpn}=6, MQS_A=36, MQS_{A×Vpn}=1, while notation is kept consistent throughout.","feedbackGuidance":"If df are swapped or MQS computed from wrong denominator, restate which factor gets p-1 numerator df and which gets (N−1)(p−1) denominator df in one-factor RM ANOVA. Emphasize notation consistency (df_A, df_{A×Vpn}, MQS_A, MQS_{A×Vpn}).","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Evaluate the repeated-measures F test"],"title":"Decision at the F gate","type":"scenario_decision","learnerAction":"Decide accept/reject H0 and report the practical interpretation.","instructions":"Given example 1: MQS_A = 36, MQS_{A×Vpn} = 1, df_A = 2, df_{A×Vpn} = 6, critical F(2;6)=5.14 at α=0.05. Choose whether to reject H0 and write one interpretation sentence.","successCriteria":"Correct decision: reject H0 (F=36 > 5.14). Interpretation states not all condition means are equal and the repeated-measure factor has a significant effect.","feedbackGuidance":"If learner accepts H0, correct them: test logic is ratio comparison to F_crit or p-value against α. Here the observed ratio is much larger than critical. Reinforce interpreting the null as equal means across all measured times/conditions.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Check sphericity and choose corrections"],"title":"Read Mauchly and pick the right row","type":"scenario_decision","learnerAction":"Choose the inference row in SPSS for reporting and state when correction is required.","instructions":"You run RM ANOVA and get Mauchly Sig. = 0.000 for the within-subject factor. Inference rows in SPSS show 'Sphericity assumed', 'Greenhouse-Geisser', 'Huynh-Feldt', 'Untergrenze'.
Select the correct row to report and explain the consequence.","successCriteria":"Learner selects a corrected row (typically Greenhouse-Geisser by default guidance) rather than Sphericity assumed, and states: correction needed because sphericity is violated (Mauchly significant).","feedbackGuidance":"If uncorrected row is chosen, explain that a significant Mauchly test means unequal difference variances violate sphericity, so corrected df are required to avoid inflated Type I error. Emphasize reading the corresponding corrected row in SPSS output.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Apply Tukey HSD in RM context"],"title":"Post-hoc pairwise test in RM","type":"practice_task","learnerAction":"Compute Tukey HSD and mark significant pairwise differences.","instructions":"Example 1: σ̂²_{A×Vpn}=1, N=4, p=3, α=0.05, and q_crit(0.05;3;6)=4.34. Compute HSD = q_crit * sqrt(MSE/N). Compare with mean differences |M1-M2|=3.00, |M1-M3|=6.00, |M2-M3|=3.00.","successCriteria":"Computed HSD = 2.17 and all three differences are marked significant (all > 2.17), with the note that Tukey is used only when sphericity is met.","feedbackGuidance":"If HSD is too high/low, check the formula: MSE is the RM residual variance and it is divided by N (number of participants) under sqrt. If learner marks only one or none significant, re-check arithmetic and the strictness condition (greater than HSD).","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Compare repeated-measures and between-subject ANOVA"],"title":"Same scores, different design choices","type":"ordering_matching","learnerAction":"Match each design choice to the correct ANOVA component and df setup.","instructions":"Use the same ad-spot ratings (4 cases × 3 spots) but compare:
A) RM design (same 4 participants rate all 3 spots),
B) Between-subject design (12 participants, 4 per spot).
Match: error term, denominator df, and expected power implication.","successCriteria":"Correct matches: A) error = residual (A×Vpn), df = 6; B) error = within, df = 9. Also notes A usually higher power because person variance is explicitly modeled/removed from residual.","feedbackGuidance":"If learner confuses between-design df with RM df, show that between-subject df within = N_total − p (or p*(n-1)) while RM within-person error df = (N−1)(p−1). Clarify why RM removes stable person differences, reducing residual noise.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Compute and report repeated-measures effect size"],"title":"Compute partial eta squared","type":"practice_task","learnerAction":"Calculate eta_p^2 and add one caution for interpretation.","instructions":"Using example 1 values QS_A=72 and QS_{A×Vpn}=6, compute η_p^2 = QS_A / (QS_A + QS_{A×Vpn}) and add one sentence on comparability of effect sizes.","successCriteria":"Correct η_p^2 = 0.923 and includes a caution such as: RM and non-RM effect sizes are not directly comparable across studies because variance decomposition differs.","feedbackGuidance":"If formula is wrong (e.g., using QS_total), correct to η_p^2 = QS_A / (QS_A + QS_{A×Vpn}) for the RM factor. If no caution is added, emphasize the source warning that cross-design effect-size comparison is restricted/problematic.","sourceConfidence":"high"},{"objectiveIds":["Write APA-like ANOVA result statements"],"title":"APA-style reporting pass","type":"rubric_answer","learnerAction":"Write a concise APA-like results paragraph from the RM ANOVA and post-hoc results.","instructions":"Draft a 2–4 sentence report for the repeated-measures example with factor 'Versuch': include M means, F-test, and Tukey HSD interpretation. blocks.body: Given a dataset, identify whether observations are linked to the same cases across conditions and decide if repeated-measures ANOVA is the appropriate design choice.
blocks.title: 1. Recognize repeated-measures designs

blocks.body: This section is grounded in the attached sources and moves the learner toward practical use: Given a dataset, identify whether observations are linked to the same cases across conditions and decide if repeated-measures ANOVA is the appropriate design choice.
blocks.title: Source-grounded explanation

blocks.body:
Classify each vignette as repeated-measures or between-subjects, and write one short justification sentence for each label.

1) 4 participants solve the same puzzle in attempt 1, 2, and 3.
2) 36 participants are split into 3 groups; each group watches only one ad spot once and gives one rating.
3) 5 judges each rate the same 3 job applications on attractiveness.
4) 20 students take pretest and posttest on anxiety with the same scale.
blocks.title:
Classify each vignette as repeated-measures or between-subjects, and write one short justification sentence for each label.

1) 4 participants solve the same puzzle in attempt 1, 2, and 3.
2) 36 participants are split into 3 groups; each group watches only one ad spot once and gives one rating.
3) 5 judges each rate the same 3 job applications on attractiveness.
4) 20 students take pretest and posttest on anxiety with the same scale.

blocks.body: Use the linkage rule: repeated-measures ANOVA is for repeated observations on the same unit (same person, same judge, or same case measured in multiple conditions/times), which creates dependency of scores. Between-subjects is used when each condition has its own distinct participants/cases and observations can be treated as independent across conditions.

blocks.body: Common error: mixing up column means with row means. Recompute: A1, A2, A3 are means of each Versuch across all participants; P1–P4 are means per participant across all three attempts. Γ is the average of all 12 cells (equivalently mean of all As or all Ps): 5.5. Correct matches are Γ=5.5, A1=8.5, A2=5.5, A3=2.5, P1=6, P2=4, P3=8, P4=4. Use this check when any value feels misplaced, especially values that repeat (4 and 5.5).

blocks.title: 3. Decompose total variation in RM ANOVA

blocks.body: This section is inferred from course preparation and should be checked against stronger source material.
blocks.title: Source-grounded explanation

blocks.body:
Using Example 1 (N = 4 persons, p = 3 time points), compute the repeated-measures ANOVA components:

a) QS_A
b) QS_{A×Vpn}

Data:
- Attempt means Ā_i: attempt 1 = 8.5, attempt 2 = 5.5, attempt 3 = 2.5
- Person means P̄_m: Vp1 = 6, Vp2 = 4, Vp3 = 8, Vp4 = 4
- Grand mean G = 5.5

Use:
QS_A = N · Σ(A_i − G)^2
QS_{A×Vpn} = Σ Σ [x_im − (A_i + P_m − G)]^2

Data matrix x_im:
Vp1: 10, 5, 3
Vp2: 6, 4, 2
Vp3: 11, 9, 4
Vp4: 7, 4, 1

Also write a short interpretation of what each term represents in the variance decomposition.
blocks.title:
Using Example 1 (N = 4 persons, p = 3 time points), compute the repeated-measures ANOVA components:

a) QS_A
b) QS_{A×Vpn}

Data:
- Attempt means Ā_i: attempt 1 = 8.5, attempt 2 = 5.5, attempt 3 = 2.5
- Person means P̄_m: Vp1 = 6, Vp2 = 4, Vp3 = 8, Vp4 = 4
- Grand mean G = 5.5

Use:
QS_A = N · Σ(A_i − G)^2
QS_{A×Vpn} = Σ Σ [x_im − (A_i + P_m − G)]^2

Data matrix x_im:
Vp1: 10, 5, 3
Vp2: 6, 4, 2
Vp3: 11, 9, 4
Vp4: 7, 4, 1

Also write a short interpretation of what each term represents in the variance decomposition.

blocks.body: Correct use of this decomposition requires separating treatment-related variation from person-adjusted residual variation: QS_A captures systematic changes across attempts, while QS_{A×Vpn} captures deviations not explained by that systematic pattern plus person-specific adjustment. A common error is using x_im − A_i or x_im − G as residual terms; the correct residual baseline is x_im(expected) = A_i + P_m − G.

blocks.body: Check the repeated-measures ANOVA rule first: factor A uses df_A = p - 1, and the within-person residual interaction uses df_{A×Vpn} = (N - 1)(p - 1). Then compute each MQS by dividing its own QS by its own df. If you swap these df or divide by the wrong denominator, you'll invert the F-logic.

So MS_A = 36 and MS_{A×Vpn} = 1, and F_crit(2,6) at α = .05 is 5.14. Which conclusion is correct about H0: μ1 = μ2 = μ3?
blocks.title: You are writing up Example 1 of a repeated-measures ANOVA (3 conditions, 4 participants). The computed values are MQS_A = 72 with df_A = 2 and MQS_{A×Vpn} = 6 with df_{A×Vpn} = 6. So MS_A = 36 and MS_{A×Vpn} = 1, and F_crit(2,6) at α = .05 is 5.14. Which conclusion is correct about H0: μ1 = μ2 = μ3?

blocks.body: Always compute F_A = MS_A/MS_error and compare it to F_crit with the same df (2,6). If F_A exceeds critical, reject H0 and interpret as not all repeated-condition means are equal.

The "Tests of Within-Subjects Effects" rows for the within-subject factor are: Sphericity assumed (df = 3, 18, p = .014), Greenhouse-Geisser (df = 1.8, 10.8, p = .041), Huynh-Feldt (df = 2.1, 12.6, p = .022), and Lower bound (df = 1, 6, p = .180). Which row should you use for inference about the factor effect?

blocks.body: You should always let the Mauchly result guide row selection: p ≤ .05 means variance-covariance assumptions for sphericity are violated, so uncorrected degrees of freedom are unsafe. Use a corrected row (here: Greenhouse-Geisser) to keep the significance decision valid.

# Statistik: Vertiefung **Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung** Studiengang Wirtschaftspsychologie Prof. Dr. Anja Dieckmann Hochschule Aalen logo # Übersicht 1. **Einführung** 2. Quadratsummen und Bestimmung der Varianzen [residualvarianz= Fehler (nur SPSS)] 3. F-Test 4. Voraussetzungen für Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung 5. Rechenbeispiel [verbundene stichproben= abhängige stichproben] 6. Vergleich mit einfaktorieller Varianzanalyse (ohne Messwiederholung) 7. Effektstärke 8. Post-hoc-Analysen 9. Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung in Statistik-Software 10. Weitere Varianzanalysen mit Messwiederholung 11. Berichten der Ergebnisse von Varianzanalysen in wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten 12. Testwahl-Quiz Hochschule Aalen logo # Messwiederholung * Man spricht von Messwiederholung, wenn verschieden Daten zu einem „Fall“ gehören, d.h. wenn diese Daten sinnvoll einander zugeordnet werden können * Beispiele: - Messwiederholung im engeren Sinn: Dieselbe AV wird mehrfach zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten erhoben (→ Veränderungsmessung) – z.B. Messung von Depressivität vor einer Therapie, direkt danach, und einige Monate später - Vpn werden mehrere Beurteilungsobjekte (z.B. Produkt A, Produkt B, Produkt C) vorgelegt, die auf der gleichen AV bewertet werden - AV wird durch unterschiedliche Verfahren erhoben (→ Vergleich der Verfahren) – z.B. Erfassung der Verträglichkeit in Selbstauskunft vs. Auskunft von Familienangehörigen auf gleicher Skala - Personen aus zwei (oder mehreren) Stichproben werden einander zugeordnet – z.B. Testwahl-Quiz # Hypothesen **Nullhypothese:** * Alle Mittelwerte der verschiedenen Messzeitpunkte sind gleich: $$ H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_p $$ * Oder: Die Effekt-Varianz von (Messwiederholungs-) Faktor A ist Null: $$ H_0: \sigma^2_{Faktor A} = 0 $$ **Alternativhypothese:** * Mindestens zwei Messzeitpunkt-Mittelwerte sind verschieden: $$ H_1: \mu_i \neq \mu_j \text{ (für mindestens ein Paar i, j)} $$ * Oder: Die Effekt-Varianz von (Messwiederholungs-) Faktor A ist größer Null: $$ H_1: \sigma^2_{Faktor A} > 0 $$ Hochschule Aalen logo # F-Test * **Haupteffekt A (Messzeitpunkt):** $$ F_A(df_A; df_{A \times Vpn}) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_A^2}{\hat{\sigma}_{A \times Vpn}^2} $$ In unserem Beispiel: $$ \hat{\sigma}_{A \times Vpn}^2 = 1 \text{ ; } \hat{\sigma}_A^2 = 36 $$ $$ \rightarrow F_{A(2;6)} = \frac{36}{1} = 36 \text{ sign.} $$ da 36 größer als krit. activityBriefs.feedbackGuidance: If a learner misclassifies a design, clarify that repeated-measures requires linked observations for the same unit across conditions (same participant, same judge, same person measured multiple times). Between-subject designs require different participants per condition and independent observations. Emphasize that the core diagnostic is dependency versus independence of scores.
activityBriefs.instructions:
Read the four vignettes and choose the design for each:
1) 4 participants solve the same puzzle in attempt 1, 2, and 3.
2) 36 participants are split into 3 groups; each group watches only one ad spot once and gives one rating.
3) 5 judges each rate the same 3 job applications on attractiveness.
4) 20 students take pretest and posttest on anxiety with the same scale.
For each, write one justification sentence.
activityBriefs.learnerAction: Classify each study vignette as repeated-measures or between-subjects.
activityBriefs.successCriteria: All four vignettes classified correctly: 1, 3, and 4 as repeated-measures; 2 as between-subjects, with justifications mentioning repeated observations per same case for RM designs.

If the learner subtracts wrong expected value, remind the residual formula is x_im - (Ai + Pm - G), not x_im - Ai or x_im - G alone.

activityBriefs.feedbackGuidance: If learner accepts H0, correct them: test logic is ratio comparison to F_crit or p-value against α. Here the observed ratio is much larger than critical. Reinforce interpreting the null as equal means across all measured times/conditions.
activityBriefs.instructions: Given example 1: MQS_A = 36, MQS_{A×Vpn} = 1, df_A = 2, df_{A×Vpn} = 6, critical F(2;6)=5.14 at α=0.05. Choose whether to reject H0 and write one interpretation sentence.
activityBriefs.learnerAction: Decide accept/reject H0 and report the practical interpretation.

activityBriefs.feedbackGuidance: If uncorrected row is chosen, explain that a significant Mauchly test means unequal difference variances violate sphericity, so corrected df are required to avoid inflated Type I error. Emphasize reading the corresponding corrected row in SPSS output.
activityBriefs.instructions:
You run RM ANOVA and get Mauchly Sig. = 0.000 for the within-subject factor. Inference rows in SPSS show 'Sphericity assumed', 'Greenhouse-Geisser', 'Huynh-Feldt', 'Untergrenze'.
Select the correct row to report and explain the consequence.
activityBriefs.learnerAction: Choose the inference row in SPSS for reporting and state when correction is required.
activityBriefs.successCriteria: Learner selects a corrected row (typically Greenhouse-Geisser by default guidance) rather than Sphericity assumed, and states: correction needed because sphericity is violated (Mauchly significant).

assumptions: The course design assumes the learner can read and interpret small arithmetic table layouts and can distinguish level-specific means (condition/person/overall). It assumes no missing-data remediation is required for the core manual examples (except acknowledging that in repeated-measures designs missing any time-point removes that case). It also assumes the course will stay within the source’s one-factor repeated-measures scope unless explicitly doing the contrast to one-way between-subject ANOVA, and that reporting examples should follow the source’s notation and APA-like F-test style.

coursePreparation.activityMixPreference: Balanced: recall and sequencing for core formulas, followed by calculation tasks and applied interpretation/reporting; include at least one decision/diagnostics activity on when to apply corrections.
coursePreparation.audience: Undergraduate psychology/social science students (especially Wirtschaftspsychologie) with prior inferential statistics knowledge
coursePreparation.constraints: Use only concepts and procedures present in the supplied source document. Prioritize one-factor repeated-measures ANOVA and its comparison to one-way between-subject ANOVA. Keep notation consistent for QS/MQS/df/F. Anchor examples to the supplied datasets and SPSS-style outputs.
coursePreparation.depth: intermediate-advanced applied focus with moderate computational detail and reporting conventions
coursePreparation.desiredOutcome: Learners can compute, interpret, and report one-way repeated-measures ANOVA and related between-subject contrasts, including variance decomposition (QS/MQS), degrees of freedom, F ratio, assumption checks (especially sphericity), corrections if assumptions fail, and post-hoc interpretation.
coursePreparation.priorKnowledge: Basic descriptive statistics, null-hypothesis testing, t-test logic, one-way between-subject ANOVA, interpretation of p-values and df, and introductory SPSS use.

checklist: Classify vignette 1 as repeated-measures (the same participants are measured repeatedly across attempts).
Classify vignette 2 as between-subjects (different participants in each ad condition; no participant appears in more than one condition).
Classify vignette 3 as repeated-measures (the same judges provide multiple linked ratings across the same set of applications).
Classify vignette 4 as repeated-measures (the same students are measured twice on the same outcome scale).

Provide one justification for each vignette that explicitly uses the dependency rule: repeated-measures requires observations linked to the same unit; between-subjects requires independent observations across conditions.
interaction.feedback: Use the linkage rule: repeated-measures ANOVA is for repeated observations on the same unit (same person, same judge, or same case measured in multiple conditions/times), which creates dependency of scores. Between-subjects is used when each condition has its own distinct participants/cases and observations can be treated as independent across conditions.
interaction.prompt:
Classify each vignette as repeated-measures or between-subjects, and write one short justification sentence for each label.

1) 4 participants solve the same puzzle in attempt 1, 2, and 3.
2) 36 participants are split into 3 groups; each group watches only one ad spot once and gives one rating.
3) 5 judges each rate the same 3 job applications on attractiveness.
4) 20 students take pretest and posttest on anxiety with the same scale.

interaction.feedback: Check the repeated-measures ANOVA rule first: factor A uses df_A = p - 1, and the within-person residual interaction uses df_{A×Vpn} = (N - 1)(p - 1). Then compute each MQS by dividing its own QS by its own df. If you swap these df or divide by the wrong denominator, you'll invert the F-logic.
interaction.prompt: For Example 1, match each formula to its correct numeric value. Use N = 4, p = 3, QS_A = 72, and QS_{A×Vpn} = 6. Keep notation consistent.

interaction.feedback: Common error: mixing up column means with row means. Recompute: A1, A2, A3 are means of each Versuch across all participants; P1–P4 are means per participant across all three attempts. Γ is the average of all 12 cells (equivalently mean of all As or all Ps): 5.5. Correct matches are Γ=5.5, A1=8.5, A2=5.5, A3=2.5, P1=6, P2=4, P3=8, P4=4. Use this check when any value feels misplaced, especially values that repeat (4 and 5.5).
interaction.prompt:
Match each symbol to the correct mean from the Tower-of-Hanoi repeated-measures data.
Data (Vp × Versuch):
Vp1: 10, 5, 3
Vp2: 6, 4, 2
Vp3: 11, 9, 4
Vp4: 7, 4, 1
Tip: A_i are column means (condition means), P_m are row means (person means), and Γ is the grand mean of all 12 values.

choices.consequence: You would report uncorrected degrees of freedom and risk overstating significance because the sphericity assumption is violated.
choices.feedback: Wrong: with significant Mauchly p, the default (uncorrected) row is not appropriate. Sphericity is violated, so corrections are required.
choices.text: Use the Sphericity assumed row; it is the default row and therefore the reported one.

choices.consequence: You report a conservative correction-based test and avoid inflated Type I error when sphericity is violated.
choices.feedback: Correct: a significant Mauchly test indicates violating sphericity, so corrected inference is required. Greenhouse-Geisser is the standard first correction row in SPSS for reporting.
choices.text: Use the Greenhouse-Geisser row; report its corrected df and p value.

choices.consequence: You might be tempted to use a less conservative correction, but in this situation the task expects the standard corrected row first.
choices.feedback: Huynh-Feldt is also a correction method, but learners should default to Greenhouse-Geisser unless there is a specific reason and course guidance to choose otherwise.
choices.text: Use the Huynh-Feldt row because it is usually closer to the uncorrected result and therefore better.

choices.consequence: You would choose an overly conservative row that is generally a fallback and not the standard reporting choice here.
choices.feedback: Lower bound is a correction option, but it is typically used only as an extreme bound, not the usual reporting row when Mauchly is significant.
choices.text: Use the Lower bound row because it is the most conservative and therefore safest.

interaction.feedback: You should always let the Mauchly result guide row selection: p ≤ .05 means variance-covariance assumptions for sphericity are violated, so uncorrected degrees of freedom are unsafe. Use a corrected row (here: Greenhouse-Geisser) to keep the significance decision valid.
interaction.justificationPrompt: In 1–2 sentences, explain which row you selected and why sphericity violation changes the row choice.
interaction.scenario: You run a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with 4 time points and inspect SPSS output. Mauchly’s test for sphericity is significant: Sig = 0.000. The "Tests of Within-Subjects Effects" rows for the within-subject factor are: Sphericity assumed (df = 3, 18, p = .014), Greenhouse-Geisser (df = 1.8, 10.8, p = .041), Huynh-Feldt (df = 2.1, 12.6, p = .022), and Lower bound (df = 1, 6, p = .180). Which row should you use for inference about the factor effect?

checklist: Compute QS_{A×Vpn} from the 12 residuals using x_im − (A_i + P_m − G), squared and summed, to get 6.
Explain that QS_A is the systematic effect/variation of the repeated-measures factor (time/measurement occasion).
Explain that QS_{A×Vpn} is the within-person residual variation after accounting for person baseline and occasion mean (person-adjusted residual/error component), not simple person variance.
Do not compute residuals with x_im − A_i or x_im − G alone; expected value must be A_i + P_m − G.
interaction.feedback: Correct use of this decomposition requires separating treatment-related variation from person-adjusted residual variation: QS_A captures systematic changes across attempts, while QS_{A×Vpn} captures deviations not explained by that systematic pattern plus person-specific adjustment. A common error is using x_im − A_i or x_im − G as residual terms; the correct residual baseline is x_im(expected) = A_i + P_m − G.
interaction.prompt:
Using Example 1 (N = 4 persons, p = 3 time points), compute the repeated-measures ANOVA components:

a) QS_A
b) QS_{A×Vpn}

Data:
- Attempt means Ā_i: attempt 1 = 8.5, attempt 2 = 5.5, attempt 3 = 2.5
- Person means P̄_m: Vp1 = 6, Vp2 = 4, Vp3 = 8, Vp4 = 4
- Grand mean G = 5.5

Use:
QS_A = N · Σ(A_i − G)^2
QS_{A×Vpn} = Σ Σ [x_im − (A_i + P_m − G)]^2

Data matrix x_im:
Vp1: 10, 5, 3
Vp2: 6, 4, 2
Vp3: 11, 9, 4
Vp4: 7, 4, 1

Also write a short interpretation of what each term represents in the variance decomposition.

choices.consequence: Decision: reject H0 and proceed as if the factor changes the outcome.
choices.feedback: Correct. Use the F-ratio: F_A = 36 / 1 = 36. Because 36 > 5.14, the null is rejected.
choices.text: Reject H0. The repeated-measures factor has a significant effect; at least two condition means differ (report significance).

choices.consequence: Decision: report no difference between conditions.
choices.feedback: Not correct. The decision depends on the test statistic, not visual impression. Here the ratio is clearly above the critical value.
choices.text: Fail to reject H0 because the differences in means look small in practice.

choices.consequence: Decision: treat the result as non-significant.
choices.feedback: The F value is MS_A divided by MS_error, not the inverse. F = 36, not 1/36.
choices.text: Fail to reject H0 because 1/36 = 0.028 and this is too small.

choices.consequence: Decision: still reject but with a wrong comparison rule.
choices.feedback: Wrong rule. For F-tests, larger-than-critical values support rejection. Reversal of the inequality is a common error.
choices.text: Reject H0 only when F_A is smaller than F_crit (or equal), since larger would mean unstable estimates.

interaction.feedback: Always compute F_A = MS_A/MS_error and compare it to F_crit with the same df (2,6). If F_A exceeds critical, reject H0 and interpret as not all repeated-condition means are equal.
interaction.justificationPrompt: In one sentence, state the F comparison (36 vs 5.14) and what this means for the repeated-measures factor.
interaction.scenario: You are writing up Example 1 of a repeated-measures ANOVA (3 conditions, 4 participants). The computed values are MQS_A = 72 with df_A = 2 and MQS_{A×Vpn} = 6 with df_{A×Vpn} = 6. So MS_A = 36 and MS_{A×Vpn} = 1, and F_crit(2,6) at α = .05 is 5.14. Which conclusion is correct about H0: μ1 = μ2 = μ3?

objectives.capability: Given a dataset, identify whether observations are linked to the same cases across conditions and decide if repeated-measures ANOVA is the appropriate design choice.
objectives.title: Recognize repeated-measures designs

objectives.capability: Compute Γ (grand mean), Â_i (condition means), and ᵃP_m (person means) from a repeated-measures table and use them in later SS calculations.
objectives.title: Compute RM means from wide data
objectives.topicName: Mittelwerte (Grand mean, condition means, person means)

objectives.capability: Calculate QS_A and QS_{A×Vpn} using the source formulas and explain what systematic and residual components each SS term represents.
objectives.title: Decompose total variation in RM ANOVA

objectives.capability: Compute df_A, df_{A×Vpn}, MQS_A, and MQS_{A×Vpn} for given N and p, and maintain consistent notation throughout.
objectives.title: Compute df and mean squares

objectives.capability: Compute F_A from mean squares, compare it to critical F at α = .05, and interpret acceptance/rejection of H0 in applied language.
objectives.title: Evaluate the repeated-measures F test

objectives.capability: Interpret Mauchly’s test output and select the correct SPSS row for inference (uncorrected vs Greenhouse-Geisser/ Huynh-Feldt/ lower-bound) when needed.
objectives.title: Check sphericity and choose corrections

# Statistik: Vertiefung **Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung** Studiengang Wirtschaftspsychologie Prof. Dr. Anja Dieckmann Hochschule Aalen logo # Übersicht 1. **Einführung** 2. Quadratsummen und Bestimmung der Varianzen [residualvarianz= Fehler (nur SPSS)] 3. F-Test 4. Voraussetzungen für Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung 5. Rechenbeispiel [verbundene stichproben= abhängige stichproben] 6. Vergleich mit einfaktorieller Varianzanalyse (ohne Messwiederholung) 7. Effektstärke 8. Post-hoc-Analysen 9. Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung in Statistik-Software 10. Weitere Varianzanalysen mit Messwiederholung 11. Berichten der Ergebnisse von Varianzanalysen in wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten 12. Testwahl-Quiz Hochschule Aalen logo # Messwiederholung * Man spricht von Messwiederholung, wenn verschieden Daten zu einem „Fall“ gehören, d.h. wenn diese Daten sinnvoll einander zugeordnet werden können * Beispiele: - Messwiederholung im engeren Sinn: Dieselbe AV wird mehrfach zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten erhoben (→ Veränderungsmessung) – z.B. Messung von Depressivität vor einer Therapie, direkt danach, und einige Monate später - Vpn werden mehrere Beurteilungsobjekte (z.B. Produkt A, Produkt B, Produkt C) vorgelegt, die auf der gleichen AV bewertet werden - AV wird durch unterschiedliche Verfahren erhoben (→ Vergleich der Verfahren) – z.B. Erfassung der Verträglichkeit in Selbstauskunft vs. Auskunft von Familienangehörigen auf gleicher Skala - Personen aus zwei (oder mehreren) Stichproben werden einander zugeordnet – z.B. Geschwister: Vergleich sozialer Kompetenz nach Geburtsreihenfolge (Erstgeborene, Sandwich-Kinder, Nesthäkchen) * Besonderheit wiederholter Messung: Die zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten erhobenen Daten sind voneinander abhängig → Voraussetzung für ANOVA ohne Messwiederholung verletzt # Einfaktorielle Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung * Erweiterung des *t*-Tests für abhängige Stichproben * Simultaner Vergleich beliebig vieler Messzeitpunkte – nur ein Test, keine $\alpha$-Kumulierung **Datenbeispiel 1:** * Vier Versuchspersonen bearbeiten Turm-von-Hanoi-Problemlöseaufgabe dreimal hintereinander * AV: Zeit bis zur Lösung in min * Frage: Hat die Wiederholung einen Effekt auf die Bearbeitungszeit? Bzw.: Unterscheiden sich Mittelwerte der Versuche voreinander?
Versuch 1 Versuch 2 Versuch 3
Vp1 10 5 3
Vp2 6 4 2
Vp3 11 9 4
Vp4 7 4 1
Hochschule Aalen logo # Einfaktorielle Varianzanalyse mit Messwdhlg.: Vor und Nachteile Vorteile: * Es werden weniger Versuchspersonen benötigt, da dieselben Vpn mehrmals getestet werden * Messwiederholung ermöglicht Erfassung der Personenvarianz (z.B. Unterschiede in Problemlösefähigkeiten) $\rightarrow$ Verringerung der Residualvarianz, da Vpn mit sich selbst verglichen werden können $\rightarrow$ höhere Teststärke (Power) Nachteile: * Zirkularitätsannahme: - Varianzen der Differenzen zweier Faktorstufen müssen gleich sein - Bei einer Verletzung der Zirkularitätsannahme erfolgt z.B. „Greenhouse-Geisser“-Korrektur des *F*-Tests * Sequenzeffekte (Reihenfolge der Testung kann auch unerwünschte Einflüsse auf AV haben) * Fehlende Daten zu einem Messzeitpunkt führen dazu, dass Vp komplett (zu allen Messzeitpunkten) ausgeschlossen werden muss Hochschule Aalen logo # Übersicht 1. Einführung 2. **Quadratsummen und Bestimmung der Varianzen** 3. F-Test 4. Voraussetzungen für Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung 5. Rechenbeispiel 6. Vergleich mit einfaktorieller Varianzanalyse (ohne Messwiederholung) 7. Effektstärke 8. Post-hoc-Analysen 9. Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung in Statistik-Software 10. Weitere Varianzanalysen mit Messwiederholung 11. Berichten der Ergebnisse von Varianzanalysen in wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten 12. Testwahl-Quiz Hochschule Aalen logo # Einfaktorielle Varianzanalyse mit Messwdhlg.: Varianzzerlegung * Gründe für Unterschiedlichkeit der Messwerte: - Systematische Variation, die auf die experimentelle Variation und damit die Unterschiede zwischen den drei Messzeitpunkten zurückgeht (Faktor A) - Unsystematische, Residualvarianz innerhalb der Vpn - Systematische Variation zwischen Versuchspersonen: Personenvarianz Diagram showing the decomposition of total variance (Gesamtvarianz) into between-person (Zwischen Personen) and within-person (Innerhalb Personen) variance, with within-person further split into Factor A and Residual. * Auf Populationsebene gilt: $$\sigma_{gesamt}^{2} = \sigma_{Vpn}^{2} + \sigma_{Faktor A}^{2} + \sigma_{Residual}^{2}$$ * Residualvarianz setzt sich zusammen aus WW zwischen Personen-faktor und Stufen des Messwiederholungfaktors A sowie unsystematische Einflüsse („Fehler“): $$\sigma_{Residual}^{2} = \sigma_{Faktor A \times Vpn}^{2} + \sigma_{Error}^{2}$$ $\rightarrow$ Nicht voneinander zu trennen, Personenfaktor kann nicht systematisch variiert werden Hochschule Aalen logo # Schätzung der Varianzen aus der Stichprobe
Quadratsumme Residual: Freiheitsgrade Residual: Residualvarianz:
$$ QS_{A \times Vpn} = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sum_{m=1}^{N} [x_{im} - (\bar{A}_i + \bar{P}_m - \bar{G})]^2 $$ $$ df_{A \times Vpn} = (N - 1) \cdot (p - 1) $$ $$ \hat{\sigma}^2_{A \times Vpn} = \frac{QS_{A \times Vpn}}{df_{A \times Vpn}} $$
Quadratsumme Faktor A: Freiheitsgrade Faktor A: Effektvarianz Faktor A:
$$ QS_A = N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{p} (\bar{A}_i - \bar{G})^2 $$ $$ df_A = p - 1 $$ $$ \hat{\sigma}^2_A = \frac{QS_A}{df_A} $$
Faktor A= Gesetzte Wiederholung Faktor A= Übun/Messwiederholung Hochschule Aalen logo physikalische grenzen (Fall)Übungseffekte (Durchschnitt PmFalsch??) # Schätzung der Residualvarianz, Beispiel 1 durchschnitt der person pro runde

* Erwartungswert: $$ E(\hat{\sigma}^2_{A \times Vpn}) = \sigma^2_{Residual} = \sigma^2_{Faktor A \times Vpn} + \sigma^2_{Error} $$ * Schätzung der Residualvarianz über Abweichung der Messwerte von erwarteten Werten aufgrund von Messzeitpunkt-MW und Personen-MW was für person typisch ist gesamtmittelwert $$ x_{im(erwartet)} = \bar{A}_i + \bar{P}_m - \bar{G} $$ $$ QS_{A \times Vpn} = \sum_{i=1}^p \sum_{m=1}^N [x_{im} - (\bar{A}_i + \bar{P}_m - \bar{G})]^2 = [10 - (8.5 + 6 - 5.5)]^2 + [5 - (5.5 + 6 - 5.5)]^2 + \dots $$ $$ + [1 - (2.5 + 4 - 5.5)]^2 = 1 + 1 + \dots + 0 = 6 $$ $$ df_{A \times Vpn} = (\overset{\text{personen}}{N - 1}) \cdot (p - 1) = (4 - 1) \cdot (3 - 1) = 3 \cdot 2 = 6 $$ $$ \hat{\sigma}^2_{A \times Vpn} = \frac{QS_{A \times Vpn}}{df_{A \times Vpn}} = \frac{6}{6} = 1 $$ messzeitpunkte (hier: 3) xim ist abhängige variable der person m zum messzeitpunkt i Hochschule Aalen logo # Schätzung der systematischen Varianz von Faktor A, Beispiel 1

* Exakte Personenvarianz spielt für Auswertung der Varianzanalyse keine Rolle, daher Konzentration auf Messwiederholungs-Faktor A * Erwartungswert: $$ E(\hat{\sigma}_A^2) = N \cdot \sigma_{Faktor A}^2 + \sigma_{Residual}^2 = $$ $$ = N \cdot \sigma_{Faktor A}^2 + \sigma_{Faktor A \times Vpn}^2 + \sigma_{Error}^2 $$ $$ QS_A = N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{p} (\bar{A}_i - \bar{G})^2 = 4 \cdot [(8.5 - 5.5)^2 + (5.5 - 5.5)^2 + (2.5 - 5.5)^2] = 4 \cdot (9 + 0 + 9) = 72 $$ $$ df_A = p - 1 = 2 $$ $$ \hat{\sigma}_A^2 = \frac{QS_A}{df_A} = \frac{72}{2} = 36 $$ # Übersicht 1. Einführung 2. Quadratsummen und Bestimmung der Varianzen 3. **F-Test** 4. Voraussetzungen für Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung 5. Rechenbeispiel 6. Weitere Varianzanalysen mit Messwiederholung 11. Berichten der Ergebnisse von Varianzanalysen in wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten 12. Testwahl-Quiz # Hypothesen **Nullhypothese:** * Alle Mittelwerte der verschiedenen Messzeitpunkte sind gleich: $$ H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_p $$ * Oder: Die Effekt-Varianz von (Messwiederholungs-) Faktor A ist Null: $$ H_0: \sigma^2_{Faktor A} = 0 $$ **Alternativhypothese:** * Mindestens zwei Messzeitpunkt-Mittelwerte sind verschieden: $$ H_1: \mu_i \neq \mu_j \text{ (für mindestens ein Paar i, j)} $$ * Oder: Die Effekt-Varianz von (Messwiederholungs-) Faktor A ist größer Null: $$ H_1: \sigma^2_{Faktor A} > 0 $$ Hochschule Aalen logo # F-Test * **Haupteffekt A (Messzeitpunkt):** $$ F_A(df_A; df_{A \times Vpn}) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_A^2}{\hat{\sigma}_{A \times Vpn}^2} $$ In unserem Beispiel: $$ \hat{\sigma}_{A \times Vpn}^2 = 1 \text{ ; } \hat{\sigma}_A^2 = 36 $$ $$ \rightarrow F_{A(2;6)} = \frac{36}{1} = 36 \text{ sign.} $$ da 36 größer als krit. F wert * Kritischer F-Wert für $\alpha = 5\%$: $$ \color{red}{F_{krit(2;6;95\%)} = 5.14} $$

Hochschule Aalen logo # Zirkularitätsannahme * Varianzen der Differenzen zweier Faktorstufen müssen gleich sein * Dies wird durch den Mauchly-Test auf Spherizität überprüft, der von SPSS automatisch bei einer ANOVA mit Messwiederholung mitgeliefert wird * Nullhypothese des Mauchly-Tests auf Spherizität lautet: $$ \sigma^2_{Messung1-Messung2} = \sigma^2_{Messung2-Messung3} = \sigma^2_{Messung1-Messung3} $$ * Wird das Ergebnis nicht signifikant ($p > .05$), bedeutet das, dass sich die Varianzen nicht signifikant voneinander unterscheiden $\rightarrow$ Zirkularitätsannahme erfüllt, keine Korrektur nötig * Wird das Ergebnis signifikant ($p \leq .05$), bedeutet das, dass sich die Varianzen signifikant voneinander unterscheiden $\rightarrow$ Korrekturverfahren * In SPSS „Greenhouse-Geisser“-Verfahren: Korrektur der Freiheitsgrade der Signifikanzprüfung; ist der Mauchly-Test signifikant, müssen die Ergebnisse in der entsprechenden Zeile des Outputs abgelesen werden Hochschule Aalen logo # Übersicht 1. Also, there was a significant main effect of response medium, $F(1, 86) = 5.14, p < 0.05, \eta_p^2 = 0.06$.
